Dynamic recommendation has traditionally been framed as a balance between long‑term user preferences and short‑term sequential patterns. Early work modeled the former with latent factorization (e.g., matrix factorization) and the latter with Markov chains, then unified them into a single objective that jointly learns user‑item affinities and item‑to‑item transitions, thereby capturing both persistent tastes and immediate context [S2:fea7e2bcbe852bcb33ce70a4d57664e954f0e82a]. A related line of research factorized personalized Markov chains directly for next‑basket prediction, emphasizing the sequential dependence of items within a shopping session [S2:50d85cb114f7c5e779a6772f2931e77dddd54a5e].

More recent approaches have turned to graph‑structured representations to encode the evolving collaborative signals among users and items. Dynamic graph neural networks (DGNNs) treat each user’s interaction sequence as a temporally evolving subgraph, allowing the model to propagate information across concurrent user sequences and capture dynamic collaborative effects that static sequence models miss [S2:286d2e0f3d882a37f486623c716d8a54a4a58fdc]. Session‑based recommendation has been enhanced with random‑walk based graph traversal (S‑Walk), which efficiently aggregates inter‑session item relationships while preserving scalability [S2:2be2e23c1ba6c2c62a85ac2ab7968d5e657ed8c6]. Continuous‑time formulations further integrate temporal collaborative signals via a temporal graph collaborative transformer, unifying sequential patterns with time‑aware graph embeddings to improve recommendation quality [S2:3418602757a13aa3abcb850d6ffba9ff930b3784]. Graph‑based embedding smoothing techniques also exploit semantic item relations and variable impact of past behaviors, refining item representations in a sequential context [S2:b9915d00a7f46e51e587aff4365e1c48ab8ef496].

The latest generation of models augments graph‑based sequential recommendation with advanced representation learning. Contrastive learning combined with knowledge‑graph embeddings has been proposed to enrich sequential recommendation by aligning user‑item interaction sequences with external semantic graphs, thereby mitigating sparsity and enhancing personalization [S2:ba372779197f9efe91ba11a46ebef78c4deb3588]. Bootstrapped latent recommendation frameworks further leverage graph structures to iteratively refine latent factors, improving robustness in dynamic environments [S2:0c607d4b88c1fd094a90c7fc0d379087141a8ba5]. Comparative studies of heterogeneous versus homogeneous GraphSAGE variants demonstrate that neighbor sampling and aggregation strategies critically affect performance on movie recommendation tasks, highlighting the importance of graph heterogeneity in capturing complex user‑item interactions [S2:13109adf6edd2d222605ec5cd1d12fe6c18f2fff].

A comprehensive survey of graph neural network applications underscores that GNN‑based recommender systems consistently outperform traditional collaborative‑filtering baselines, particularly when modeling dynamic, multi‑relational data such as social links, knowledge graphs, and temporal interaction streams [S2:1be97c1d9ace0363f8f612ca1be3d4fb33e177bb]. Collectively, these works illustrate a clear trajectory: from static factorization and Markov models toward dynamic, graph‑centric architectures that jointly capture sequential behavior, temporal evolution, and rich relational context, setting the stage for next‑generation recommendation systems.
